Succeeding John XXIII, this pontiff carried the Second Vatican Council to its 1965 close and built historic bridges with Eastern Orthodox and Protestant churches — who was he?
Pope Paul VI: Head of the Catholic Church from 1963 to 1978.

She served as France's Minister of Justice under Sarkozy before later becoming Minister of Culture across four different governments, and has been mayor of one of Paris's arrondissements since 2008. Who is this French politician?
Declared independent on a man-made platform in the Adriatic in 1968, this micronation used Esperanto as its official language before being demolished by Italian authorities — what was it called?
Republic of Rose Island: 1968 micronation in the Adriatic Sea. The Italian government viewed it as a ploy by Rosa to raise money from tourists while avoiding national taxation.
Born in Tampico, Illinois, this future actor started as a sports broadcaster in Iowa in 1933 before moving to Hollywood and later serving as Screen Actors Guild president twice. Who was he?
Ronald Reagan: President of the United States from 1981 to 1989.
Taken as a Mughal hostage at age nine to enforce his father's treaty, this man later ruled from 1681 to 1689 as the second king of a major Indian empire — who is he?
Sambhaji: Chhatrapati of the Marathas from 1681 to 1689.
Nicknamed "the Grim," this Ottoman sultan grew his empire by seventy percent in just eight years, conquering the entire Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt between 1516 and 1517 — who was he?
Selim I: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1512 to 1520.
After a 1969 coup, this army commander became Somalia's third president and reconstituted the country as a one-party Marxist-Leninist state — who is he?
Siad Barre: President of Somalia from 1969 to 1991.

Traditionally blamed on Queen Catherine de' Medici, this 1572 wave of Catholic mob violence targeted Huguenots gathered in Paris for a royal wedding during the French Wars of Religion. By what name is it known?
St. Bartholomew's Day massacre: 1572 killing of Huguenots in France.
Nicknamed for both his towering height and his 23-year run, this architect of the 'Swedish Model' welfare state holds the record as his country's longest-serving prime minister — who was he?
Tage Erlander: Prime Minister of Sweden from 1946 to 1969.
Of African descent through his mother, this French Revolutionary Wars general was one of only a handful of men of color to command European troops as a general officer in that era — who is he?
This Mitsubishi engineer had the extraordinarily unlucky distinction of being caught in both the Hiroshima and Nagasaki atomic bombings in August 1945 — and lived to tell about it. Who is he?
Tsutomu Yamaguchi: Japanese atomic bombing survivor.
This French Romantic giant gave the world both 'The Hunchback of Notre-Dame' and a sprawling 1862 novel that became a beloved musical — who was he?
Victor Hugo: French writer and politician (1802–1885)
Beginning in April 2014 with a Russian-backed uprising in eastern Ukraine, this conflict ended only when it was swallowed by the full-scale 2022 invasion — what was it called?
War in Donbas: 2014–2022 war between Ukraine and Russia.

A German Army intelligence officer in occupied Warsaw during WWII, this man is credited with saving several Polish Jews, including pianist Władysław Szpilman — his story was dramatized in The Pianist. Who was he?
Wilm Hosenfeld: German army officer (1895–1952) and Righteous among the Nations.
Having previously served as Japan's Foreign Minister and Chief Cabinet Secretary, which LDP politician became Minister for Internal Affairs and Communications in October 2025?
Which one below was born first?
John Ray (born 1627) is the earliest of the four. John Ray (29 November 1627 – 17 January 1705) was an English Christian naturalist and one of the earliest English parson-naturalists.
Which one below was born first?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four. After helping found Shu Han, Zhuge Liang exercised near-total authority over both civil and military affairs.
Which of these four is the oldest?
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is an astronomer?
Jabir ibn Hayyan is an astronomer. The c. 215 treatises that survive today mainly deal with alchemy and chemistry, magic, and Shi'ite religious philosophy.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
What is the atomic number of Rhodium?
Rhodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rh and atomic number 45.
What is the atomic number of Argon?
Argon is a chemical element; it has symbol Ar and atomic number 18.
In what year was Carlos Slim born?
Carlos Slim Helú (Spanish: [ˈkaɾlos esˈlin eˈlu, - esˈlim -]; born 28 January 1940) is a Mexican business oligarch, investor and philanthropist.
In what year was Antoine Lavoisier born?
Antoine Lavoisier: It is generally accepted that Lavoisier's great accomplishments in chemistry stem largely from his changing the science from a qualitative to a quantitative one.
In what year was Travis Kalanick born?
Travis Kalanick: Travis Cordell Kalanick (born August 6, 1976) is an American businessman best known as the co-founder and former chief executive officer (CEO) of Uber.
In what year did Zhuge Liang die?
Zhuge Liang: After helping found Shu Han, Zhuge Liang exercised near-total authority over both civil and military affairs.
In what year did Marie Curie die?
Marie Curie: Curie was born in Warsaw, Russian Empire, where she studied at the clandestine Flying University and began her practical scientific training.
In what year was LSD discovered?
LSD taken orally has an onset of action of 0.4 to 1.0 hours and a duration of 7 to 12 hours.
TeX: Donald Knuth. TeX is a popular means of typesetting complex mathematical formulae; it has been noted as one of the most sophisticated digital typographical systems.
Tupolev Tu-204: Kazan Aircraft Production Association. It was developed for Aeroflot as a replacement for the medium-range Tupolev Tu-154 trijet in the 1990s.
In which country is British Aerospace 146?
British Aerospace 146: United Kingdom. Production figures include the Avro RJ, an improved version from Avro International Aerospace, a subsidiary of BAE Systems.
Who is credited with discovering Fructose?
Fructose: Augustin-Pierre Dubrunfaut. Fructose, or fruit sugar, is a common monosaccharide, i.e. a simple sugar.
Who is credited with discovering LSD?
LSD: Albert Hofmann. LSD taken orally has an onset of action of 0.4 to 1.0 hours and a duration of 7 to 12 hours.
Who is credited with discovering Manganese?
Manganese: Johan Gottlieb Gahn. Manganese is a chemical element; it has the symbol Mn and atomic number 25.

This mosquito species, native to tropical Southeast Asia and marked with distinctive white bands on its legs and body, has spread worldwide via international trade and travel, becoming a significant public health concern — what species is it?

Aedes albopictus (synonym Stegomyia albopicta), from the mosquito (Culicidae) family, also known as the (Asian) tiger mosquito or forest mosquito, is a species of mosquito native to the tropical and subtropical areas of Southeast Asia.
This parasitic intestinal illness, caused by Entamoeba histolytica, can produce cysts that survive for weeks in soil or nearly an hour under fingernails — what is it called?
Amoebiasis is an infection of the intestines caused by a parasitic amoeba Entamoeba histolytica.
Most often caused by stroke or head trauma, which condition impairs a person's ability to comprehend or formulate language because specific brain regions aren't working?
Aphasia is an impairment in a person's ability to comprehend or formulate language because of dysfunction in specific brain regions.
This gram-positive, spore-forming bacterium was the first ever proven experimentally to cause disease, laying the groundwork for germ theory in 1876 — which microbe?
Bacillus anthracis is a gram-positive and rod-shaped bacterium that causes anthrax, a deadly disease to livestock and, occasionally, to humans.

First flickering to life in octocorals some 540 million years ago and evolving independently at least 94 separate times, this glow is sometimes borrowed from symbiotic bacteria — what is the phenomenon?
Bioluminescence is the production of light by an organism as the result of a chemiluminescence reaction.
Whose book Atlas of the Heart became an HBO Max documentary series in 2022, following an earlier Netflix film about her work on courage?
Brené Brown (born November 18, 1965) is an American academic, author and podcaster.
Prized in India for hashish and cultivated from China to West Africa, this Hindu Kush-native plant produces cannabinoid levels well above ordinary hemp — which species?
Cannabis indica is an annual plant species in the family Cannabaceae indigenous to the Hindu Kush mountains of Southern Asia.

A member of the poppy family found across Europe and western Asia, this herbaceous plant is nicknamed 'greater celandine' and isn't actually related to the similarly-named 'lesser celandine' — what's its scientific name?
Chelidonium majus is a perennial herbaceous flowering plant in the poppy family Papaveraceae.

Native to western South America, this shrub bears oval leaves and red berries, and when its leaves are chewed or brewed as tea they act as a mild stimulant with no evidence of addiction — which plant is it?
Coca refers to any of the four cultivated plants in the family Erythroxylaceae, native to western South America.
Belonging to the same genus as poliovirus and echovirus, these enteroviruses enter cells with help from a shared receptor and commonly cause aseptic meningitis — which pathogens?

Coxsackievirus are a few related enteroviruses that belong to the Picornaviridae family of nonenveloped, linear, positive-sense, single-stranded, RNA viruses, as well as its genus Enterovirus, which also includes poliovirus and echovirus.
Used to treat ADHD and narcolepsy, this 'right-handed' mirror-image form of a stimulant molecule is also misused to boost cognitive and athletic performance — what is it?
Dextroamphetamine is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant and enantiomer of amphetamine that is used in the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy.
Along with the platypus, this quill-covered Australian and New Guinean mammal is one of only two living egg-laying mammal groups, and its young are adorably called puggles — what is it?
Echidna are quill-covered monotremes (egg-laying mammals) belonging to the family Tachyglossidae, living in Australia and New Guinea.
This American investor and podcaster coined the phrase 'intellectual dark web' and proposed a physics framework called 'Geometric Unity' — who is he?
Eric Weinstein (born October 26, 1965) is an American investor and podcast host.
This plant genus of roughly 850 species includes woody trees, vines, and epiphytes native to the tropics, though only two species are widely cultivated for their sweet fruit — what genus is it?
Ficus (or) is a genus of about 850 species of woody trees, shrubs, vines, epiphytes and hemiepiphytes in the family Moraceae.

This Austrian engineer founded a firearms company in 1963; when his first pistol entered Austrian service in 1982, its famous model number referred to his 17th patent, not the rounds it held — who is he?
Prince Carl Philip, Duke of Värmland
Gaston Glock (19 July 1929 - 27 December 2023) was an Austrian engineer and businessman.

Dating back roughly 250 million years to the early Triassic, these ground-dwelling herbivorous insects use powerful hind legs to leap away from danger and hatch as nymphs that molt five times — what's the insect?
Grasshopper are a group of insects belonging to the suborder Caelifera.
This naturally occurring molecule and medication is a powerful blood anticoagulant used to treat heart attacks and prevent clotting in dialysis machines and test tubes — what is it?
Heparin (UFH), is a medication and naturally occurring glycosaminoglycan.
This endocrine condition floods the body with thyroid hormone, causing a racing heart, heat intolerance, tremor, and weight loss — and a rare 'storm' can be deadly; what is it?
Hyperthyroidism is a endocrine disease in which the thyroid gland produces excessive amounts of thyroid hormones.

From deep-sea gribbles to the woodlice under your garden stones, members of this crustacean order share seven pairs of jointed limbs and brood their young in a pouch called a marsupium — what is the order?
Isopoda is an order of crustaceans. The order is divided into eleven suborders.
Famed first for studying diamagnetism, which Irish physicist proved in 1859 the link between atmospheric CO2 and what we now call the greenhouse effect?
John Tyndall (2 August 1820 - 4 December 1893) was an Irish physicist.

Named after a French mathematician but reportedly learned from his Swiss tutor, this calculus theorem evaluates tricky limits by taking derivatives of the numerator and denominator — what is it called?
L'Hôpital's rule (loh-pee-TAHL) is a mathematical theorem used for evaluating the limit of a quotient of two functions, each of which tends to zero or infinity, by taking each function's derivative.
Serving as a somatosensory organ as well as a tool for eating and forming sounds, this pair of soft facial features is one of the most visible parts of the mouth — what are they?
Lip are a horizontal pair of soft appendages attached to the jaws and are the most visible part of the mouth of many animals, including humans.
Roughly 60% the diameter of Pluto and stained reddish-brown by tholins, this trans-Neptunian dwarf planet carries minor-planet number 136472 — what is it?
Makemake (minor-planet number 136472) is a dwarf planet orbiting the Sun in the Kuiper belt, a disc of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Triggered by falling progesterone, this monthly discharge from the uterine lining signals that pregnancy hasn't occurred and typically first arrives at "menarche" between ages 11 and 13 — what is it?
Menstruation (also known as a period, among other colloquial terms) is the regular discharge of blood and mucosal tissue from the inner lining of the uterus through the vagina.
This Nissin Food Products founder invented instant chicken ramen and went on to create the Top Ramen and Cup Noodles brands — who is he?

Momofuku Ando (March 5, 1910 - January 5, 2007), born Go Pek-Hok (Peh-e-j: G Pek-hok; Ti-l: Go Pik-hok), was a Taiwanese-born, ethnic Chinese, Japanese inventor and businessman who founded Nissin Food Products Co., Ltd.

Nicknamed for its terrifying rate of tissue destruction, this fast-spreading bacterial infection doesn't actually consume flesh — the bacteria instead release toxins that destroy it — what is this disease called?
Necrotizing fasciitis (NF), also known as flesh-eating disease or flesh-eating bacteria, is an infection that kills the body's soft tissue.
Named after a German physicist, this SI unit of electrical resistance is represented by the uppercase Greek letter omega — name the unit?
Ohm (symbol:, the uppercase Greek letter omega) is the unit of electrical resistance in the International System of Units (SI).
Found in organs such as the brain and lungs, inside flatworms, and within leaf cross-sections, this word names an organism's bulk functional tissue — what is it?
Parenchyma is the bulk of functional substance in an animal organ such as the brain or lungs, or a structure such as a tumour.

This insect order's scientific name derives from the Ancient Greek word for 'apparition' or 'phantom' — fitting for a group whose members are famous for disguising themselves as twigs and leaves. What order is this?
Phasmatodea (also known as Phasmida or Phasmatoptera) are an order of insects whose members are variously known as stick insects, stick bugs, walkingsticks, stick animals, or bug sticks.

This large, nearly ubiquitous family of flowering plants provides the world's cereal crops, bamboo, and the plants used in lawns and pastures, ranking as the fifth-largest plant family with roughly 12,000 species — what family is this?
Poaceae (poh-(y)e), also called Gramineae (gr-(y)e), is a large and nearly ubiquitous family of monocotyledonous flowering plants commonly known as true grasses.
This Eurasian fruit tree, also called the cherry plum, is believed to be one of the ancestral parents of the plum we cultivate today — what species is it?
Prunus cerasifera is a species of plum known by the common names cherry plum and myrobalan plum.

Rooted in Minangkabau cooking, this dish slow-simmers meat in spiced coconut milk until the oil separates and it fries in its own glaze — both a method and a meal across the Malacca Strait; what is it?

Rendang is a fried meat or dry curry made of meat stewed in coconut milk and spices, widely popular across Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, and the southern parts of the Philippines, where each version is considered local cuisine.
First identified in Wuhan, this positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus prompted the WHO to declare a global health emergency from January 2020 to May 2023 — what's its name?
SARS-CoV-2 (SARSCoV2) is a coronavirus that causes COVID-19, the respiratory illness responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic that began in late 2019.
Born into a Russian-Jewish family in Moscow and brought to the US at age six, which co-founder of Google served as president of Alphabet until 2019?
Sergey Brin (born August 21, 1973) is an American computer scientist and businessman who co-founded Google with Larry Page.
Made simply from ice mixed with fruit juice or purée, plus the occasional splash of wine or honey, this dairy-free frozen treat goes by what name?
Sorbet is a frozen dessert made using ice combined with fruit juice, fruit pure, or other ingredients, such as wine, liqueur, or honey.
Developed from an earlier design, this variable-sweep-wing Soviet fighter-bomber served from 1967 to 1990 and was exported in variants like the Su-22 — which aircraft is it?
Sukhoi Su-17 (NATO reporting name: Fitter) is a variable-sweep wing fighter-bomber developed for the Soviet military.
Also called bush crickets, this insect family in the suborder Ensifera includes over 8,000 mostly nocturnal, leaf-mimicking species — which family?
Tettigoniidae are commonly called katydids (especially in North America) or bush crickets.
Usually caused by mutations in the TCOF1 gene, which autosomal dominant condition affects facial bone and ear development but not intelligence?
Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS) is a genetic disorder characterized by deformities of the ears, eyes, cheekbones, and chin.
Once classified in the honeysuckle family before molecular studies gave it its own, this genus of 150-plus shrub species reaches Africa only via the Atlas Mountains — which genus?
Viburnum is a genus of about 150-175 species of flowering plants in the family Viburnaceae.
Marketed under names like Rompun, this veterinary sedative and alpha-2 adrenergic agonist is often combined with ketamine for animal anesthesia and used as an emetic in cats — what is it?

Xylazine is a structural analog of clonidine and an 2-adrenergic receptor agonist, sold under many trade names worldwide, most notably the Bayer brand name Rompun, as well as Anased, Sedazine and Chanazine.
Known by the common name yarrow, this pungent, fernleaved plant in the daisy family is used in traditional medicine and as livestock feed — what is its scientific name?
Achillea millefolium: Species of plant. Achillea millefolium, commonly known as yarrow or common yarrow, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae.
A former IMF economist, this politician has served as President of Ivory Coast since 2010 after earlier stints as the country's prime minister in the early 1990s — who is he?
Alassane Ouattara: President of Ivory Coast since 2010. Ouattara became the president of the Rally of the Republicans (RDR), an Ivorian political party, in 1999.
Native to the Americas, this plant is better known by its common names common ragweed, annual ragweed, or low ragweed — what is its scientific name?
Ambrosia artemisiifolia: Species of flowering plant in the daisy family.

Named from Greek words meaning "unlike other shrimp," this extinct arthropod from the Burgess Shale had swimming flaps, big compound eyes and grasping frontal appendages, reaching over a foot long — which prehistoric predator?
Anomalocaris: Extinct genus of cambrian radiodont.

Known only from fragmentary remains including vertebrae and a giant femur first found by a farmer in 1987, this titanosaur may be the largest land animal ever discovered, stretching up to 35 meters — which genus?
Argentinosaurus: Late Cretaceous giant sauropod dinosaur genus.
The famous AL 288-1 skeleton nicknamed 'Lucy,' unearthed in Ethiopia's Afar region, belongs to which extinct East African hominin species that lived roughly 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago?
Australopithecus afarensis: Extinct hominid from the Pliocene of East Africa.
This inflammatory condition causes recurring, painful mouth sores along with eye inflammation and arthritis, and is diagnosed after at least three sore outbreaks in a year — which condition?
Behçet's disease: Inflammatory disorder. Behçet's disease or Behçet's syndrome (BD; sometimes written Behcet) is a type of inflammatory disorder which affects multiple parts of the body.
This medium-sized antelope of India and Nepal sports corkscrew horns up to 30 inches long and a striking two-tone coat, with white around the eyes set against black face stripes — which animal?
Blackbuck: Antelope native to India and Nepal. The blackbuck (Antilope cervicapra), also known as the Indian antelope, is a medium-sized antelope native to India and Nepal.
Nicknamed 'murderer's thumb' or 'stubbed thumb,' this genetic trait gives about 2% of people a short, rounded thumb linked to the HOXD13 gene — what is it?
Brachydactyly type D: Abnormal shortening of the distal part of the thumb.
Alongside HTML and JavaScript, which style sheet language handles the layout, colors, and fonts of a webpage — separating presentation from content?
CSS: Style sheet language. CSS is a cornerstone technology of the World Wide Web, alongside HTML and JavaScript.

Time called her the "literary godmother" to Paris's Lost Generation, and her Black Sun Press printed early Hemingway and Henry Miller — but she also patented the first successful modern bra. Who was she?
Usually arising from damage to the developing brain before birth, this group of childhood movement disorders causes stiff or weak muscles, tremors, and poor coordination — what condition?
Cerebral palsy: Movement disorders that appear in early childhood.
Selected from over 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space Project, this Concord, New Hampshire educator died aboard the Challenger in 1986 — who was she?
Christa McAuliffe: American teacher and astronaut (1948–1986)

This ancient insect order traces back to the Late Jurassic, with chewing-mouthpart ancestors called "roachoids" scuttling around some 320 million years ago — yet only about 30 of its 4,600 species ever moved in with us. Which creature is it?
Cockroach: Insects of the order Blattodea.

Used in Chinese medicine for over 1,500 years, this genus of parasitic fungi infects insects and other arthropods, taking its name from Greek and Latin words meaning 'club' and 'head' — which genus is it?
Cordyceps: Genus of fungi. Cordyceps is a genus of ascomycete fungi (sac fungi) that includes over 260 species worldwide, many of which are parasitic.

Commonly called sowbread, this genus of 25 tuberous flowering plants is prized for upswept petals and patterned leaves, native from the Mediterranean to Iran with one species even found in Somalia — which genus?
Cyclamen: Genus of flowering plants in the primrose family.
This autoimmune disease attacks both the skin and skeletal muscles, causing a rash alongside worsening weakness, and is often linked to distinct myositis-specific autoantibodies — which condition?
Dermatomyositis: Autoimmune disease of skin and muscle. Dermatomyositis (DM) is a group of sytemic autoimmune inflammatory diseases primarily affecting the skin and skeletal muscles.
Developed as a 14-bed sleeper upgrade of an earlier airliner, which low-wing propeller monoplane cruised at 207 mph and reshaped air travel from the 1930s through World War II?
Douglas DC-3: Airliner and military transport aircraft family.
Capable of delivering shocks up to 860 volts, this South American knifefish helped inspire the invention of the battery in 1800 — what is it?
Electric eel: Genus of fishes in South America.
Also called rocket or arugula, this sharp-flavored leaf vegetable native to the Mediterranean and Asia is a popular salad green in the cabbage family — which plant?
This burrowing mammal builds ever-expanding tunnel systems, and its saliva contains toxins that paralyze its favorite prey, earthworms — what animal is it?
European mole: Species of mammal. The European mole (Talpa europaea) is a mammal of the order Eulipotyphla.
The discipline that studies money, currency, assets, and liabilities, divided into personal, corporate, and public branches — what is this field of study called?
Finance: Academic discipline studying businesses and investments.

Coated in cornmeal and pan-cooked while still unripe, this dish was originally a Northeastern and Midwestern staple before a hit movie rebranded it as quintessentially Southern comfort food — what is it?
Fried green tomatoes: American dish. Fried green tomatoes is a culinary dish usually found in the United States, made from unripe (green) tomatoes coated with cornmeal and fried.

Arriving late to a lecture, this mathematician copied down two famous unsolved problems in statistics, mistook them for homework — and solved them; he's better known for inventing the simplex algorithm for linear programming. Who was he?

This German engineer invented the high-speed petroleum engine, working alongside his lifelong partner Wilhelm Maybach to build small, fast motors they hoped to mount on any kind of vehicle. Who was he?
Gottlieb Daimler: German engineer, industrialist and automotive pioneer (1834–1900)
Often translated as 'Jewish law' but literally meaning 'the way of walking,' this body of religious rules draws on the Torah, the Talmud, and codes like the Shulchan Aruch — what is it called?
Halakha: Jewish rabbinical law. Halakha is often translated as "Jewish law", although a more literal translation might be "the way one proceeds" or "the way of walking".
This German-American statistician patented an electromechanical punched-card tabulating machine in 1884, founding a company that would eventually be renamed IBM — who was he?
Herman Hollerith: American statistician and inventor. Hollerith founded a company that was amalgamated in 1911 with several other companies to form the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company.

This fatal inherited neurodegenerative disorder, once called a 'chorea,' starts with subtle mood changes before bringing on uncoordinated, dance-like involuntary movements as the basal ganglia degrade — what is it?
Huntington's disease: Inherited neurodegenerative disorder. Huntington's disease (HD), also known as Huntington's chorea, is a fatal neurodegenerative disease that is usually inherited.
Formed by the merger of two hip flexor muscles that join at the femur's lesser trochanter, this is the body's strongest flexor of the hip — what is it called?
Iliopsoas: Joined psoas and iliacus muscles of the hip and thigh.
Native to Africa and Eurasia, this opportunistic canid can sustain a running pace of about 10 mph over long distances while hunting small mammals, birds, and reptiles — which animal?
As a Princeton grad student this mathematician dreamed up an "equilibrium" concept that won him a 1994 Nobel in Economics — who was he?
John Forbes Nash Jr.: American mathematician and Nobel Laureate (1928–2015)
Smaller, seedier, and more aromatic than its Persian cousin, this citrus hybrid lends its tart flavor to a beloved Florida pie named after the island chain it's associated with — what is it?
Key lime: Citrus fruit and plant.
This probability principle explains why a casino might lose money on a single spin of roulette but reliably earns a predictable percentage over many thousands of spins. What is it called?
Law of large numbers: Averages of repeated trials converge to the expected value.
Instrumental in the discovery of nuclear fission, this Austrian-Swedish physicist fled Nazi Germany in 1938 after losing her post under the Nuremberg Laws — who is she?

Fired by IBM in 1968 for revealing her intent to transition — an apology that took until 2020 — this computer scientist had already invented dynamic instruction handling behind modern out-of-order execution. Who was she?
Lynn Conway: American computer scientist and electrical engineer (1938–2024)

Originally hoping to become an engineer, this Italian physician became one of the first women to graduate from medical school in Italy and later devised an influential educational philosophy — who is she?
Maria Montessori: Italian physician and educator (1870–1952)
Comprising 18 to 24 species that hybridize freely where their ranges overlap, this genus of the mint family thrives in wet, moist soils worldwide — what is it?
Mentha: Genus of flowering plants in the family Lamiaceae.
This twin-engine Soviet fighter, known to NATO as 'Fulcrum,' was built in the 1970s to counter American jets like the F-15 and F-16 — which aircraft is it?
Mikoyan MiG-29: Soviet twin-engine jet fighter aircraft. The Mikoyan MiG-29 (Russian: Микоян МиГ-29; NATO reporting name: Fulcrum) is a twin-engine fighter aircraft designed in the Soviet Union.

Synthesized in 2003 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna and named in 2016 for the Russian region around it, this element 115 has a most-stable isotope lasting just 0.65 seconds — what is it?
Moscovium: Chemical element with atomic number 115 (Mc)

As modern science emerged, this concept came to mean the passive reality moved by divine laws — and after the Industrial Revolution, the part of the world untouched by intentional human hands. What word is it?
Nature: Material world and its phenomena.
Born in New York to Holocaust-survivor parents, this political scientist made the politics of the Holocaust and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict his life's work. Who is he?
This medical specialty trains physicians for four years after medical school to diagnose, medically treat, and surgically correct eye disease — what is it?
Ophthalmology: Field of medicine treating eye disorders.
Credited as the 'father of toxicology,' this Swiss Renaissance physician and alchemist also wrote prophetic 'Prognostications' later studied by Rosicrucians — who is he?
Paracelsus: Swiss physician, philosopher, theologian, and alchemist (c. 1493 – 1541)
Known for its speed, this large crow-sized raptor has a blue-grey back, barred white underparts, and a black head — an avivore with marked sexual dimorphism — what is it?
Peregrine falcon: Fastest known animal and common bird of prey.
This branch of biology studies how organs, cells, and biomolecules carry out their functions, and gives its name, alongside medicine, to a Nobel Prize category — which field?
Physiology: Science regarding functions in organisms or living systems.
Native to Southeast Asia and tasting like a sweet grapefruit, this non-hybrid citrus is the largest of them all — in fact, an ancestor of both the grapefruit and the bitter orange — what is it?
Pomelo: Citrus fruit from Southeast Asia.
Created in the early 18th century, this dark pigment was the first modern synthetic color, made by oxidizing iron ferrocyanide salts — what is it?
Prussian blue: Synthetic pigment. Prussian blue (also known as Berlin blue, Brandenburg blue, Parisian and Paris blue) is a dark blue pigment produced by oxidation of ferrous ferrocyanide salts.
Element 88 reacts with nitrogen rather than oxygen in air, turning black, and once glowed in self-luminous paints despite being highly carcinogenic — which element is it?
Radium: Chemical element with atomic number 88 (Ra)
Curving around the chest, these bones protect the lungs and heart and, in snakes, support and protect the whole body — what are they called?
Rib: Long bone in vertebrates that protects vital respiratory and cardiovascular organs.
First identified in Wuhan in late 2019 and once provisionally called 2019-nCoV, this positive-sense RNA virus is the one that causes COVID-19 — what's its official name?
SARS-CoV-2: Virus that causes COVID-19. The virus previously had the provisional name 2019 novel coronavirus (2019-nCoV), and has also been called human coronavirus 2019 (HCoV-19 or hCoV-19).
After early family-friendly Christian games found little success, which developer switched to horror in 2014 and created a hit franchise of horror video games?
Scott Cawthon: American video game developer (born 1978)
In this inherited blood disorder, faulty haemoglobin warps red cells into a rigid crescent shape that can't bend through capillaries, causing painful blockages — what is it?
Also known as milo, jowar, or Guinea corn, this grass — domesticated in Sudan and now grown worldwide — ranks as the fifth most important cereal crop on Earth — which grain?
Sorghum: Species of grain. It is typically an annual, but some cultivars are perennial.
